С момента запуска вакцин от коронавируса в социальных сетях распространились многочисленные недостоверные сведения и теории заговора. Недавний пост, распространявшийся в интернете, делает два важных утверждения: в первую очередь, что вакцины от COVID-19 не прошли стандартные этапы тестирования, включая испытания на животных, и что общество использовалось в качестве «лабораторных крыс»; во-вторых, что существует тайное соглашение между Pfizer и правительством Израиля, запрещающее Израилю раскрывать информацию о побочных эффектах в течение 15 лет, а также что вакцина не может быть введена людям с различными заболеваниями, курящим, ожиревшим или ведущим половую активность в течение месяца после вакцинации. В данной статье подробно рассматриваются эти утверждения и предоставляется фактический контекст.

**Утверждение 1: Вакцины от COVID-19 не прошли необходимые этапы тестирования, включая испытания на животных**

Утверждение о том, что вакцины от COVID-19 не прошли необходимые этапы тестирования, неверно. Разработка вакцин, включая вакцины от COVID-19, следует хорошо зарекомендовавшему себя процессу, включающему предклинические (на животных) исследования, а затем фазированные клинические испытания на людях. Срочность пандемии привела к ускорению сроков, но это было достигнуто за счёт перекрытия этапов испытаний и быстрого анализа данных, а не за счёт пропуска этапов.

Все основные вакцины от COVID-19, включая те, разработанные Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna и AstraZeneca, прошли испытания на животных до перехода к клиническим испытаниям на людях. Эти предклинические исследования необходимы для оценки первоначальной безопасности и иммунного ответа. Только после успешных испытаний на животных вакцины перешли к фазе 1 клинических испытаний на людях, которая сосредоточена на безопасности, а затем к более крупной фазе 2 и 3 для определения эффективности и мониторинга побочных эффектов.

Утверждение о том, что общество использовалось в качестве «лабораторных крыс», искажает строгий процесс. Хотя вакцинация больших групп населения проходила в рамках экстренных разрешений на использование, это основывалось на обширных данных, полученных от десятков тысяч участников клинических испытаний, а также на постоянном мониторинге безопасности. Глобальные регулирующие органы рассмотрели эти данные до предоставления одобрения или разрешения на использование.

**Утверждение 2: Соглашение Pfizer-Израиль и ограничения по применению вакцины**

Второе утверждение касается, якобы, секретного соглашения между Pfizer и Израилем, которое, по утверждению, запрещает Израилю раскрывать информацию о побочных эффектах в течение 15 лет и накладывает длинный список ограничений на то, кто может получить вакцину и как вести себя после вакцинации.

На самом деле, соглашение между Pfizer и Израилем было уникальным в том, что оно обеспечило раннее получение вакцины в обмен на агрегированные, анонимизированные данные о результатах вакцинации, чтобы помочь глобальному пониманию эффективности вакцины. Нет достоверных доказательств запрета на раскрытие информации о побочных эффектах в течение 15 лет. На самом деле, Израиль регулярно публикует обновления о эффективности вакцины и побочных эффектах, а его данные сыграли важную роль в формировании глобальных политики вакцинации.

Кроме того, утверждение о том, что вакцина не может быть введена людям с заболеваниями печени, легких или почек, пациентам с онкологическими заболеваниями, ожиревшим людям или курильщикам, не подтверждается официальными рекомендациями. Хотя определённые меры предосторожности могут применяться к лицам с ослабленным иммунитетом или тяжёлыми аллергиями, нет общего запрета на вакцинацию для этих групп. Утверждение о запрете на половую активность в течение месяца после вакцинации не основано и не отражено в какой-либо официальной документации или рекомендациях от Pfizer или здравоохранительных органов.

**Заключение**

Оба утверждения, распространённые в вирусном посте, являются неточными и вводящими в заблуждение. Вакцины от COVID-19 прошли необходимые этапы тестирования, включая испытания на животных, а соглашение между Pfizer и Израилем не содержит положений, ограничивающих раскрытие информации о побочных эффектах или накладывающих необычные ограничения на вакцинированных лиц. Фактобазированная информация критически важна в борьбе с недостоверной информацией, особенно в условиях глобальной публичной эпидемии.

article_content:
A recent social media post has attracted attention by making three notable claims about COVID-19 vaccines and the global vaccination effort. The claims are: (1) Some countries returned AstraZeneca vaccines in whole batches to the manufacturer because they appeared to be expired and falsified; (2) Sputnik V is the only vaccine that does not contain a virus and does not infect people; and (3) Several small countries have transferred money not to the COVAX platform, but to fraudulent intermediary companies that misappropriated the money. Here, we analyze each claim using available evidence and provide necessary context.

**Claim 1: Countries Returned Expired and Falsified AstraZeneca Vaccines**

The rollout of the AstraZeneca vaccine has faced challenges, including concerns over expiration and distribution. Several countries, particularly in Africa and Asia, have at times returned or even destroyed batches of AstraZeneca vaccines. These actions were primarily due to doses arriving close to their expiration dates, making it difficult for local health authorities to administer them in time. However, instances of entire batches being returned to the manufacturer specifically due to being both expired and "falsified" are not widely documented. There have been reports of counterfeit vaccines in the global supply chain, but these cases are relatively rare and typically involve criminal investigations, not official returns by governments. Most returns or refusals have been linked to logistical issues with expiry, not falsification. Thus, while there is some basis for concern over expired doses, the characterization of batches being returned for being “expired and falsified” overstates the documented cases.

**Claim 2: Sputnik V is the Only Vaccine That Does Not Contain a Virus and Does Not Infect People**

Sputnik V, developed by Russia’s Gamaleya Institute, is a vector vaccine that uses a harmless adenovirus to deliver genetic instructions for the coronavirus spike protein. The claim that Sputnik V is the only vaccine that "does not contain a virus and does not infect people" is inaccurate. In fact, Sputnik V does contain a virus—albeit a non-replicating adenovirus vector, which cannot cause disease. Other vaccines, such as the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna mRNA vaccines, do not contain any virus at all; instead, they use lipid nanoparticles to deliver genetic material. Additionally, none of the authorized COVID-19 vaccines, including vector vaccines and mRNA vaccines, are capable of causing COVID-19 infection, as they do not contain live SARS-CoV-2 virus. Therefore, the claim is misleading on both counts.

**Claim 3: Small Countries Lost Money to Fraudulent Intermediaries Instead of COVAX**

The COVAX initiative was set up to ensure equitable access to COVID-19 vaccines globally, with funding from governments and organizations. While COVAX intended to provide a secure purchasing platform, the urgency of the pandemic led some countries and organizations, particularly those with less negotiating power, to seek vaccines through intermediaries. There have been documented cases of fraud, where fake intermediaries promised vaccine supplies and then disappeared with advance payments, especially targeting small or less-developed countries. These incidents have been reported in multiple regions and have caused financial losses and delays in vaccination campaigns. Consequently, this claim reflects a real and well-documented problem during the vaccine rollout.

**Conclusion**

Upon reviewing the three claims, the article finds that only the third claim—relating to financial fraud during vaccine procurement—has strong factual support. The first claim about AstraZeneca returns has a partial basis but lacks evidence for widespread falsification. The second claim about Sputnik V is inaccurate, as several other vaccines do not contain virus particles and none can cause COVID-19 infection. This analysis highlights the importance of scrutinizing information circulating on social media, especially regarding public health interventions.

Štai, analizuojame kiekvieną teigą pagal prieinamą įrodymą ir pateikiamas reikiamas kontekstą.

**Teiga 1: Šalys grąžino pasibaigusias ir apvairuotas AstraZeneca vakcinas**

AstraZeneca vakcinos skirstymas patyrė kelių iššūkių, įskaitant atsiradimo datų ir skirstymo klausimus. Kelių šalių, ypač Afrikos ir Azijos šalių, kai kuriais atvejais grąžino net išgyvendino AstraZeneca vakcinos kiekius. Daugelis grąžinimų ar atsisakymų susiję su logistikos problemomis dėl iškilo datų, ne su apvairavimu. Todėl, nors yra kai kurių susirūpinimų dėl pasibaigusių dozų, kiekvienas kiekis grąžinamas dėl "pasibaigimo ir apvairavimo" pervertina dokumentuotus atvejus.

**Teiga 2: Sputnikas V yra vienintelis vakcinas, kurios nesudaro viruso ir neįkvepija žmonių**

Sputnikas V, kurį sukūrė Rusijos Gamaleja institutas, yra vektoriaus vakcina, kuri naudoja nekenksmingą adenovirusą, kad perduotų koronaviruso spike baltymų genetines instrukcijas. Teiga, kad Sputnikas V yra vienintelis vakcinas, "kurios nesudaro viruso ir neįkvepija žmonių", yra neteisinga. Tikrai, Sputnikas V turi virusą – neapvairuojantį adenoviruso vektoriaus, kuris negali sukelti ligos. Kiti vakcinai, tokie kaip Pfizer-BioNTech ir Moderna mRNA vakcinos, neturi jokio viruso, o naudoja lipidinius nanodaleles, kad perduotų genetinį medžiagą. Todėl ši teiga yra netikslus abiejose kryptimis.

**Teiga 3: Mažos šalys prarado pinigus įtartinoms perkančiųjų įmonėms, o ne COVAX**

COVAX iniciatyva buvo sukurtas užtikrinti lygį prieigos prie COVID-19 vakcinos visame pasaulyje, finansuojant valstybes ir organizacijas. Nors COVAX ketino pateikti saugų pirkimo platformą, pandemijos skubumas paskatino kelias šalis ir organizacijas, ypač tąs šalis, kurios turėjo mažiau pergalėjimo galimybių, ieškoti vakcinos per perkančiųjų. Šie įvykiai buvo pranešti keliuose regionuose ir sukėlė finansinius nuostolius ir vėlavimus vakcinacijos kampanijose. Todėl ši teiga atspindi tikrą ir gerai dokumentuotą problemą vakcinacijos skirstymo metu.

**Išvada**

Apžiūrėjus tris teigias, straipsnis randa, kad tik trečia teiga, susijusi su finansinės apvairavimo klausimais vakcinų pirkime, turi stiprų faktinį pagrindą. Pirmoji teiga apie AstraZeneca grąžinimus turi dalinį pagrindą, tačiau nėra įrodymų apie išplėstines apvairavimo atvejus. Antroji teiga apie Sputnikas V yra netikslus, nes keli kiti vakcinai neturi viruso ir nė viena negali sukelti COVID-19 infekcijos. Ši analizė pabrėžia svarbą atsargiai peržiūrėti informaciją, kuri kinta socialiniuose tinkluose, ypač dėl viešųjų sveikatos įgyvendinimų.

A video circulating on social media claims to show a "fake syringe" being used by wealthy individuals and top officials during vaccination campaigns. The post suggests that these individuals are deceiving the public by pretending to receive vaccines, while in reality, they are not being injected with any substance. This claim has generated significant public interest and concern, particularly in the context of global vaccination efforts.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to examine the context in which such videos have appeared, the nature of the syringes shown, and the motivations that might underlie the spread of such content.

First, the core claim is that a "fake syringe" is intentionally used to create the illusion that prominent figures are being vaccinated when they are not. Videos that allegedly support this claim often show syringes with retractable needles or syringes where the plunger does not appear to move. In some cases, these clips are accompanied by captions or voice-overs suggesting a deliberate attempt to mislead the public.

However, a closer examination of vaccination protocols and the equipment used reveals alternative explanations. Retractable syringes are a common medical device designed to protect healthcare workers from accidental needle-stick injuries. These syringes automatically retract the needle into the barrel after use, reducing the risk of exposure to bloodborne pathogens. This safety feature can make it appear, especially on video, as if the injection is not genuine or that the needle never penetrates the skin.

Moreover, some videos have been found to be misinterpreted or taken out of context. In several widely shared clips, officials or celebrities appear to receive a vaccine with a "fake" syringe, but further investigation often reveals that the full footage or subsequent images show a standard injection being administered. In other cases, healthcare workers have made mistakes, such as not fully depressing the syringe plunger, which have been corrected immediately afterward with a proper dose given off-camera.

It is also important to consider that vaccination campaigns targeting high-profile individuals are often conducted in public to encourage vaccine uptake and demonstrate trust in public health measures. While isolated incidents of human error or miscommunication have occurred, there is no credible evidence to support a widespread conspiracy involving the use of "fake syringes" by the rich or top officials to deceive the public.

In conclusion, while videos showing unusual syringe use have circulated widely, the claim that fake syringes are systematically used by elites to avoid vaccination is not supported by the available evidence. Most instances can be attributed to the use of legitimate safety devices, video misinterpretation, or isolated procedural errors. Public concern about transparency is understandable, but the claim of deliberate deception on a large scale is unfounded.

A recent social media post claims that “70% of French healthcare workers do not trust and reject vaccination.” This statement, if accurate, would suggest a significant crisis of confidence in vaccines among those at the forefront of the French healthcare system. In light of the ongoing global importance of vaccination, especially following the COVID-19 pandemic, it is crucial to examine the validity of this claim and understand the context behind healthcare workers’ attitudes toward vaccination in France.

First, it is important to clarify what is meant by “do not trust and reject vaccination.” This language implies both a lack of confidence in vaccines and an active refusal to receive them. Healthcare workers play a vital role in not only administering vaccines but also in advocating for their safety and effectiveness to the wider public. If a majority of these professionals were indeed distrustful and rejecting vaccination, it could have far-reaching implications for public health efforts.

Looking at available data, France has historically exhibited higher vaccine hesitancy compared to some other European countries. Surveys in the past have shown that segments of the general population, including some healthcare workers, have expressed doubts about vaccines, particularly during the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines. Early in the COVID-19 vaccination campaign, there were reports of hesitancy among French healthcare workers, with surveys suggesting that between 20% and 40% expressed reluctance or uncertainty about receiving the vaccine. Reasons cited included concerns about the rapid development of COVID-19 vaccines, potential side effects, and a general mistrust in pharmaceutical companies or governmental authorities.

However, the claim that 70% of French healthcare workers “do not trust and reject vaccination” appears to be an exaggeration not supported by current or historical data. Most surveys conducted during the height of the pandemic, and even before, do not approach this high level of distrust or rejection. In fact, as vaccine campaigns progressed and more information became available regarding vaccine safety and efficacy, acceptance rates among healthcare workers increased. By the time vaccination became mandatory for healthcare professionals in France in 2021, uptake rates rose significantly, with the vast majority of healthcare workers receiving their COVID-19 vaccinations.

It is also important to distinguish between hesitancy and outright rejection. Trust in routine vaccinations, such as those for influenza or childhood diseases, has remained relatively stable among healthcare professionals, even if some skepticism persisted regarding new vaccines.

In summary, while vaccine hesitancy and skepticism have been present among French healthcare workers, the claim that 70% do not trust and reject vaccination is not substantiated by available evidence. A recent social media post has made the claim that AstraZeneca, the pharmaceutical company behind one of the widely used COVID-19 vaccines, is in violation of the Nuremberg Code because it “represents a genetically modified organism.” This assertion has circulated widely, raising questions about the nature of the AstraZeneca vaccine, the definition of genetically modified organisms (GMOs), and the protections provided by the Nuremberg Code. Here, we examine the facts behind each part of this claim.

The AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine, also known as Vaxzevria, is based on a viral vector platform. It uses a modified version of a chimpanzee adenovirus to deliver genetic instructions into human cells, prompting an immune response against the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Specifically, the adenovirus vector has been engineered to be harmless and to carry the gene for the coronavirus spike protein, which triggers immunity.

The term “genetically modified organism” or GMO usually refers to any living organism whose genetic material has been artificially manipulated through genetic engineering, often in the context of agriculture or food. In the context of vaccines, the viral vector (the adenovirus) is genetically modified so that it can safely deliver the genetic instructions. However, the vaccine itself is not a living organism, nor does it permanently alter the recipient’s DNA. Once the adenovirus delivers the spike protein gene and the immune system responds, the vector is eliminated from the body. Thus, the person who receives the vaccine does not become a genetically modified organism.

The core of the social media claim is that using such a vaccine violates the Nuremberg Code, a set of ethical principles established after World War II to govern medical experiments involving human subjects. The Nuremberg Code emphasizes voluntary informed consent, the necessity of avoiding unnecessary physical and mental suffering, and the requirement that experiments be conducted by qualified personnel.

For a violation of the Nuremberg Code to occur, there must be a lack of informed consent or the imposition of experimental procedures without proper safeguards. The AstraZeneca vaccine underwent multiple clinical trials, regulatory review, and approval in many countries. Recipients of the vaccine are provided with information about its benefits and risks, and receiving the vaccine is voluntary in most jurisdictions. While the rapid development and emergency use authorizations of COVID-19 vaccines have sparked debate, the processes followed align with established ethical guidelines and regulatory standards.

In summary, while the AstraZeneca vaccine utilizes a genetically modified viral vector, it does not render its recipients genetically modified organisms. Furthermore, the development, approval, and distribution of the vaccine have followed ethical and regulatory standards designed to protect participants and recipients, including informed consent. Therefore, the claim that AstraZeneca violates the Nuremberg Code because it “represents a genetically modified organism” is not supported by the facts.

Vaccine ngừa COVID-19 của AstraZeneca, còn được gọi là Vaxzevria, dựa trên nền tảng vector virus. In recent days, a social media post has circulated widely, claiming that Georgia’s Health Minister said she would not receive the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. This statement has sparked debate and concern, especially as public trust in vaccination campaigns remains critical in the fight against the pandemic. To provide clarity, this article examines the veracity of the claim and provides context surrounding the events in question.

The claim originates from comments reportedly made by Ekaterine Tikaradze, who served as Georgia’s Minister of Internally Displaced Persons from the Occupied Territories, Labour, Health and Social Affairs during the crucial phases of the COVID-19 vaccine rollout in Georgia. The statement appeared during the early stages of the country’s vaccination campaign, when AstraZeneca was among the first vaccines made available in Georgia.

At the time, AstraZeneca’s vaccine had been the subject of intense scrutiny worldwide due to reports of rare blood clotting events. Several European countries had temporarily suspended its use as a precautionary measure. Against this backdrop, the Georgian government aimed to reassure a hesitant public and encourage participation in the national vaccination program.

During a press briefing in March 2021, Minister Tikaradze was asked whether she and other government officials would lead by example and receive the AstraZeneca vaccine. Minister Tikaradze confirmed that she did not plan to get the AstraZeneca shot herself. She explained that she had already recovered from COVID-19 and, according to the guidelines in place at the time, those who had recently been infected were advised to wait before being vaccinated. She further mentioned that she would receive a vaccine “when it is her turn and according to the recommendations of healthcare professionals.” However, she stopped short of explicitly refusing AstraZeneca altogether, instead framing her decision as adherence to medical guidance.

This nuanced position was quickly interpreted and, in some cases, misrepresented on social media. While it is accurate that Georgia’s Health Minister said she would not be vaccinated with AstraZeneca at that specific time, her reasoning was related to her recent recovery from COVID-19 and compliance with health protocols, rather than a categorical rejection of the AstraZeneca vaccine. In subsequent public statements, she emphasized the safety and importance of vaccination for eligible individuals.

In summary, the core claim that Georgia’s Health Minister said she would not be vaccinated with AstraZeneca is partially accurate but lacks crucial context. Minister Tikaradze’s statements were based on her personal medical situation and prevailing health guidelines, not a general condemnation of the AstraZeneca vaccine. As vaccine hesitancy continues to present challenges, providing complete and accurate information remains essential for public understanding and trust.

A recent social media post claims that “The WHO doesn’t have the answer on the safety of AstraZeneca,” raising concerns about the World Health Organization’s (WHO) position on the safety of the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Given the significant role that global health authorities play in public confidence and vaccination campaigns, it is essential to examine this claim in detail and provide an accurate assessment.

**Background and Context**

The AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine, developed in collaboration with Oxford University, has been widely administered across the world, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. It was one of the first vaccines authorized for emergency use by various national and global health agencies, including the WHO. The vaccine’s rollout, however, has not been without controversy. Rare cases of blood clotting disorders, specifically thrombosis with thrombocytopenia syndrome (TTS), were reported in a small number of recipients, prompting several countries in 2021 to temporarily pause or limit its use to certain age groups.

Throughout the vaccine’s deployment, the WHO has played a central role in reviewing emerging data, issuing recommendations, and reassuring the public about vaccine safety. The organization’s Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization (SAGE) and its Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety (GACVS) have both continually monitored and assessed the safety profile of the AstraZeneca vaccine.

**Fact-Checking the Claim**

The core claim in the social media post suggests the WHO lacks a definitive answer about the safety of the AstraZeneca vaccine. This assertion requires careful analysis.

It is true that no vaccine or medical intervention is 100% risk-free. The process of monitoring vaccine safety is ongoing, with data collection and analysis evolving as more doses are administered globally. The WHO has acknowledged the rare risk of blood clots associated with the AstraZeneca vaccine and has consistently updated its guidance based on the latest evidence. However, the organization has repeatedly stated that the benefits of the vaccine in preventing COVID-19, with its associated risks of severe disease, hospitalization, and death, far outweigh the risks of rare adverse events.

The WHO’s stance on AstraZeneca’s safety has been one of cautious reassurance. The agency has not claimed absolute certainty — an impossible standard in medicine — but has provided clear, evidence-based recommendations. It has emphasized that rare side effects are being investigated and that national authorities should weigh the benefits and risks in their respective contexts. The organization has also recommended that individuals be informed about the possibility of rare adverse events and advised to seek medical attention if symptoms arise.

**Conclusion**

The statement that “The WHO doesn’t have the answer on the safety of AstraZeneca” is misleading. While it is accurate that the WHO, like all health authorities, continues to review safety data and cannot guarantee absolute safety, the organization has issued comprehensive guidance based on the best available evidence. The WHO’s position remains that the AstraZeneca vaccine’s benefits far outweigh its risks for most populations. The characterization that the WHO lacks an “answer” overlooks the nuance and transparency involved in global vaccine safety monitoring. Rather than indicating uncertainty or ignorance, the WHO’s approach demonstrates the ongoing commitment to evidence-based recommendations and public safety.

El grup estratègic d'experts en immunització (SAGE) i el comitè consultiu global de seguretat de vacunes (GACVS) de l'organització han continuat monitorant i avaluant el perfil de seguretat de la vacuna AstraZeneca.

**Verificació de la veracitat de la declaració**

La declaració central del post de xarxes socials suggerix que l'OMS no té una resposta definitiva sobre la seguretat de la vacuna AstraZeneca. Aquesta afirmació requereix un anàlisi cuidadosa.

És cert que cap vacuna o intervenció mèdica no és del tot sense risc. El procés de monitoratge de la seguretat de la vacuna és continu, amb la recollida i anàlisi de dades que evoluciona a mesura que es fan més administracions a nivell mundial. L'OMS ha reconegut el risc raro de coagulacions associades a la vacuna AstraZeneca i ha actualitzat constantment les seves guies basant-se en la darrera evidència. No obstant això, l'organització ha repetit que els beneficis de la vacuna en la prevenció del coronavirus, amb els seus riscos associats de malaltia greu, hospitalització i mort, superen clarament els riscos d'events adversos rars.

La posició de l'OMS sobre la seguretat de AstraZeneca ha estat d'una tranquil·lització prudent. L'agència no ha afirmat cap certesa absoluta — un estàndard impossible en medicina —, però ha ofert recomanacions clares i basades en evidència. Ha subratllat que els efectes secundaris rars estan sota investigació i que les autoritats nacionals han de ponderar els beneficis i riscos en el seu context respectiu. L'organització ha recomanat també que les persones estiguin informades sobre la possibilitat d'events adversos rars i que busquin atenció mèdica si es produeixen símptomes.

**Conclusió**

La declaració que "l'OMS no té la resposta sobre la seguretat de AstraZeneca" és enganyosa. Tot i que és cert que l'OMS, com totes les autoritats de salut, continua revisant dades de seguretat i no pot garantir una seguretat absoluta, l'organització ha emesa guies completes basades en la millor evidència disponible. La posició de l'OMS segueix sent que els beneficis de la vacuna AstraZeneca superen els seus riscos per a la majoria de les poblacions. La caracterització que l'OMS no té una "resposta" ignora la nuances i la transparència implicades en la monitoració global de la seguretat de les vacunes. En lloc de reflectir incertesa o ignorància, l'abordatge de l'OMS demostra el compromís continu amb recomanacions basades en evidència i la seguretat pública.

A social media post recently claimed that vaccines contain MRC-5, pulmonary cells from aborted embryos, as well as cattle fetus and a virus found in monkeys that causes cancer. To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is important to break down each component of the claim and analyze the scientific and manufacturing processes involved in vaccine production.

First, the mention of MRC-5 refers to a specific cell line. MRC-5 cells are originally derived from lung tissue of a 14-week-old male fetus aborted in the 1960s in the UK. These cells are commonly used in laboratory settings for the growth of viruses required for vaccine production. However, it is crucial to clarify that vaccines do not contain actual MRC-5 cells or lung tissue. Rather, the cells serve as a medium in which certain vaccine viruses are grown. After the virus is harvested, the vaccine is purified to remove cellular material, so only trace amounts—if any—of residual DNA or protein may remain in the final product. This is standard practice and is subject to strict regulatory oversight.

The claim that vaccines contain "pulmonary cells from the aborted embryo" is misleading. While the original source of the MRC-5 cell line was fetal lung tissue, modern vaccines do not incorporate cells or tissue from embryos. Instead, the cell line is maintained in laboratory conditions and used solely as a vehicle for growing vaccine viruses. The cells themselves are not present in meaningful amounts in the vaccine administered to patients.

The assertion that vaccines contain "cattle fetus" likely refers to the use of fetal bovine serum (FBS) in laboratory procedures. FBS is a common supplement used to promote cell growth in culture, but it is not an ingredient in vaccines. While some cell lines might be grown in the presence of FBS, the serum is removed and the vaccine is purified before distribution. Therefore, it is inaccurate to state that vaccines contain cattle fetus material.

The final claim involves a "virus found in monkeys that causes cancer." This likely references SV40, a simian virus that was discovered as a contaminant in early polio vaccines produced using monkey kidney cells in the late 1950s and early 1960s. While SV40 has been studied for its potential link to cancer, subsequent vaccine production protocols have eliminated this risk through improved screening and purification methods. Modern vaccines do not contain SV40 or other cancer-causing viruses from monkeys.

In summary, while some vaccines are developed using cell lines that originated from fetal tissue and may involve bovine serum in their manufacturing process, the final products do not contain embryo tissue, cattle fetus material, or cancer-causing monkey viruses. The claim presented in the social media post is a misrepresentation of the complex and highly regulated process of vaccine production. Public health authorities rigorously monitor the safety and purity of vaccines to ensure that they do not contain harmful contaminants.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated claiming that the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine caused the deaths of five people in Italy, three of whom were soldiers who died as a result of thrombosis. Such statements have raised concerns and fueled debate about vaccine safety, particularly regarding the AstraZeneca vaccine, which has faced scrutiny across Europe.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to consider the timeline of AstraZeneca’s rollout in Italy, the reported incidents of adverse reactions, and how authorities have responded.

AstraZeneca's vaccine was authorized for use in the European Union in January 2021 and quickly became a central component of Italy's mass vaccination campaign. Shortly after its introduction, several European countries reported rare cases of blood clots, known medically as thrombosis, in recipients of the vaccine. Italy was among the countries where these events were investigated, with national health authorities and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) launching inquiries into possible links between the vaccine and these adverse events.

In March 2021, Italy temporarily suspended the use of a specific AstraZeneca vaccine batch after reports of deaths and serious health incidents, including cases of thrombosis. Media coverage at the time reported that a handful of individuals, including military personnel, had died shortly after receiving the vaccine. Among these, three Italian soldiers were noted to have died following vaccination, with initial autopsy reports suggesting blood clots as a possible cause.

However, subsequent investigations by Italian health authorities and the EMA found that, while there was a very rare association between the AstraZeneca vaccine and unusual blood clotting events, the overall risk remained extremely low compared to the benefits of vaccination. The reported deaths, including those of the soldiers, were thoroughly examined to establish causality. In several cases, definitive links between the vaccine and the deaths could not be established; other medical factors or underlying conditions were considered as possible contributors.

The EMA concluded that the AstraZeneca vaccine could, in rare instances, lead to serious blood clotting disorders, often accompanied by low platelet counts. These events were estimated to occur at a rate of several cases per million doses administered. As a result, some countries adjusted their recommendations, limiting AstraZeneca’s use to older age groups less at risk for such side effects.

While it is true that deaths following AstraZeneca vaccination were reported in Italy, and soldiers were among those affected, the claim that vaccination definitively “caused” these deaths oversimplifies a complex medical issue. Investigations did identify a small number of thrombosis cases linked to the vaccine, but causality in each individual case was not always clear. Authorities maintained that the benefits of vaccination in preventing COVID-19 outweighed the small risk of adverse events.

In summary, while reports of deaths, including thrombosis among soldiers, did occur following AstraZeneca vaccination in Italy, official investigations found only a rare association between the vaccine and such events. Claims that the vaccine directly caused five deaths, including three soldiers, lack full substantiation based on the available evidence and medical analysis.

In recent weeks, a social media post has circulated claiming that Sweden has issued digital vaccine certificates, and that “C.O.V.ID” stands for “Certificate Of Vaccine ID.” The post further alleges that these digital certificates are expected to be embedded subcutaneously—under the skin—and will contain personal data, including vaccination records. This article examines the accuracy of these claims and provides context around digital vaccine certification in Sweden and globally.

**Background: Vaccine Certificates in Sweden**

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries, including Sweden, have explored or implemented digital systems to verify vaccination status. These systems, often called “vaccine passports” or digital COVID certificates, are designed to facilitate safe travel, access to events, and public spaces by confirming an individual’s vaccination or testing status.

Sweden launched its digital COVID certificate in July 2021, in line with the European Union’s Digital COVID Certificate program. The certificate allows individuals to prove their COVID-19 vaccination, test, or recovery status. It is typically available as a QR code on a smartphone, as a printout, or as a PDF download. The primary goal of these certificates is to enable secure and convenient verification of health status, particularly for international travel.

**Fact-Checking the Claim:**

1. **C.O.V.ID as “Certificate Of Vaccine ID”:**
   The post claims that “C.O.V.ID” is an acronym for “Certificate Of Vaccine ID.” This is inaccurate. COVID-19 stands for “Coronavirus Disease 2019,” named by the World Health Organization after the virus SARS-CoV-2 and the year it was first identified. There is no official or governmental documentation that redefines COVID as “Certificate Of Vaccine ID.” This appears to be a misinterpretation or deliberate reimagining of the term rather than a factual description.

2. **Digital Certificates Issued in Sweden:**
   It is accurate that Sweden has issued digital COVID certificates. These certificates are part of a broader international effort to streamline the process of verifying vaccination status. The Swedish digital COVID certificate is not unique in this regard; many EU countries and others worldwide have adopted similar systems.

3. **Subcutaneous Embedding of Certificates:**
   The post asserts that digital certificates are expected to be embedded subcutaneously, containing personal data and vaccination records. There is no evidence to support this claim. Swedish authorities have not announced any plans to embed vaccine certificates under the skin. The current digital certificates are accessed via smartphones, printed documents, or digital files—none require or involve any form of subcutaneous technology. While some companies and individuals in Sweden have experimented with microchip implants for personal use, such as making payments or unlocking doors, these are voluntary and unrelated to government vaccine certification programs.

4. **Personal Data and Privacy:**
   The digital COVID certificates in Sweden, as in other EU countries, contain limited information: the person’s name, date of birth, vaccine or test details, and a digital signature. The system is designed with privacy and data protection in mind, conforming to European data protection standards.

**Conclusion:**

While Sweden has implemented digital COVID certificates, the claim that “C.O.V.ID” stands for “Certificate Of Vaccine ID” is false. There are no plans or government mandates to embed these certificates under the skin. The digital certificates remain digital or physical documents, used primarily for travel and event access, and are in line with privacy standards. The social media post contains significant inaccuracies and misrepresentations about the nature and purpose of digital vaccine certificates in Sweden.

4. **Personīgie dati un privātība:**

Sistēma tiek izstrādāta ar privātības un datu aizsardzības prasībām, atbilstot Eiropas datu aizsardzības standartiem.

**Secinājums:**

Kas attiecas uz Šveicē ieviestajiem digitālajiem COVID sertifikātiem, teikums, ka "C.O.V.ID" nozīmē "Sertifikāts vaksīnācijas identifikācijai", ir nepatiess. Digitālie sertifikāti paliek digitāli vai fiziski dokumenti, izmantojami galvenokārt ceļošanai un pasākumu piekļuvei, un tie atbilst privātības standartiem. Sociālajā tīklā izplatītā ziņa satur daudz nepatiesību un nepareizu informāciju par digitālo vaksīnācijas sertifikātu dabu un mērķi Šveicē.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that mortality rates from Pfizer and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines in the United States are "between 58% and 41% as evidenced by VAERS," suggesting that a significant proportion of people who receive these vaccines die as a result. This statement has caused concern and confusion among some members of the public. This article examines the accuracy of the claim, the background of the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS), and what is known about vaccine safety and mortality rates.

First, it is important to understand what VAERS is and how it operates. VAERS is a national early warning system co-managed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). It is designed to detect possible safety issues with vaccines by collecting reports of adverse events following vaccination from healthcare professionals, patients, and members of the public. However, VAERS is a passive surveillance system and accepts all reports without verifying whether the vaccine caused the adverse event. Reports can be submitted by anyone, and the events may be coincidental, unrelated, or misattributed.

The core claim suggests that the mortality rate from Pfizer and Moderna vaccines is alarmingly high—between 58% and 41%—and that this is supported by VAERS data. In reality, this interpretation misrepresents how VAERS data should be used. The percentage cited appears to conflate the proportion of VAERS reports that include deaths, or miscalculates the relationship between vaccine doses administered and reported deaths. In fact, the vast majority of VAERS reports do not involve death, and deaths reported to VAERS are extremely rare compared to the hundreds of millions of vaccine doses administered.

It is also crucial to note that a report of death to VAERS does not mean that the vaccine caused the death. VAERS reports can include any death that occurs after vaccination, regardless of cause. Many people receiving COVID-19 vaccines are elderly or have underlying health conditions, and deaths can occur by chance in the weeks following vaccination. Public health authorities routinely analyze these reports for patterns that might indicate a safety concern. To date, investigations of deaths reported after vaccination have not shown any causal link between the Pfizer or Moderna vaccines and unexpected deaths.

Data from the CDC and FDA show that the risk of death directly attributable to mRNA COVID-19 vaccines (Pfizer and Moderna) is extremely low. The benefits of vaccination in preventing serious illness, hospitalization, and death from COVID-19 far outweigh the very small risk of severe side effects. Both agencies continue to monitor vaccine safety closely and update the public with transparent findings.

In summary, the claim that "mortality from Pfizer and Moderna vaccines is between 58% and 41% as evidenced by VAERS" is misleading and not supported by the available evidence. VAERS is not a database of confirmed vaccine-caused deaths, and its data cannot be used to calculate mortality rates from vaccines. The scientific consensus remains that Pfizer and Moderna vaccines are safe and effective, with an extremely low risk of serious adverse events, including death.

A recent social media post has gone viral, alleging that a former employee of a hospital in Romania publicly accused the hospital of improper treatment of coronavirus patients. The post further claims that the employee admitted patients were murdered by the administration of sedative drugs, supposedly to increase the number of reported coronavirus deaths.

This article examines the veracity of these claims by analyzing publicly available information, statements from relevant authorities, and the broader context of healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic in Romania.

**Background and Context**

Romania, like many countries, faced significant challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic. Hospitals were frequently overwhelmed, resources were stretched thin, and medical staff were under immense pressure. Accusations of mismanagement or poor treatment did arise sporadically, often reflecting public anxiety and frustration with the healthcare system.

The core claim in the social media post is twofold: first, that a former employee accused a Romanian hospital of improper treatment of COVID-19 patients; and second, that this employee admitted patients were intentionally killed by administering sedatives to artificially inflate death statistics.

**Analysis of the Claims**

1. **Improper Treatment of COVID-19 Patients**

Throughout the pandemic, there were occasional reports and whistleblower statements from healthcare workers in various countries, including Romania, expressing concern over hospital conditions, lack of resources, or alleged mismanagement. In some instances, former or current employees spoke out about shortcomings in patient care, sometimes citing insufficient oxygen supplies, inadequate staffing, or outdated facilities.

However, while such criticisms were documented, they typically centered on systemic issues rather than deliberate harm or malpractice. There is no widespread or substantiated evidence that Romanian hospitals, as a matter of policy or practice, engaged in improper treatment with the intent to harm patients.

2. **Allegations of Murder and Manipulation of COVID-19 Figures**

The more serious claim—that hospital staff intentionally murdered patients using sedative drugs to increase coronavirus death figures—is an extraordinary accusation. Fact-checking efforts, reviews of Romanian media coverage, and statements from medical associations and government agencies do not support this allegation. No credible reports have documented such admissions by hospital employees, nor have authorities confirmed any investigations or findings that corroborate this scenario.

It is important to note that sedative drugs are sometimes used in intensive care settings for patients on ventilators, as part of standard medical protocols. The use of these drugs is closely monitored and intended for patient comfort, not harm.

**Conclusion**

The social media post in question amplifies a dramatic and distressing narrative that is not supported by credible evidence. While criticisms of hospital management and care standards in Romania during the COVID-19 pandemic have been raised, there are no verified reports of former employees publicly admitting to or accusing hospitals of intentionally murdering patients to manipulate coronavirus statistics. Such claims appear to be unfounded and likely to contribute to misinformation and public distrust.

Misinformation can spread rapidly, especially during times of crisis. It is essential to rely on verified information from trusted sources and to approach sensational claims with skepticism unless and until they are substantiated by credible evidence.

Rumah sakit seringkali terlalu penuh, sumber daya terbatas, dan staf medis menghadapi tekanan yang sangat besar. **Analisis Klaim**

1. **Perawatan yang Tidak Tepat terhadap Pasien Korona**

Selama pandemi, terdapat laporan dan pernyataan dari pekerja kesehatan di berbagai negara, termasuk Romani, yang menyatakan kekhawatiran terhadap kondisi rumah sakit, kurangnya sumber daya, atau pengelolaan yang dituduh tidak baik. Dalam beberapa kasus, mantan atau karyawan saat ini menyampaikan keluhan tentang kurangnya standar perawatan pasien, kadang menyebutkan pasokan oksigen yang tidak memadai, staf yang tidak cukup, atau fasilitas yang usang.

Namun, meskipun kritik tersebut terdokumentasi, biasanya berfokus pada masalah sistemik, bukan tindakan sengaja merugikan atau malpraktik. Tidak ada bukti yang luas atau terbukti bahwa rumah sakit di Romani, sebagai kebijakan atau praktik, melakukan perawatan yang tidak tepat dengan niat merugikan pasien.

2. **Tuduhan Pembunuhan dan Manipulasi Angka Korona**

Klaim yang lebih serius—bahwa staf rumah sakit sengaja membunuh pasien dengan menggunakan obat penenang untuk meningkatkan angka kematian korona—adalah tuntutan yang luar biasa. Upaya pemeriksaan fakta, tinjauan media Romani, serta pernyataan dari asosiasi medis dan lembaga pemerintah tidak mendukung tuduhan ini. Tidak ada laporan yang dapat dipercaya yang mencatat pengakuan dari karyawan rumah sakit tentang hal tersebut, dan otoritas juga tidak mengonfirmasi investigasi atau temuan yang mendukung skenario ini.

Perlu dicatat bahwa obat penenang kadang digunakan dalam pengaturan perawatan intensif untuk pasien yang menggunakan ventilator, sebagai bagian dari protokol medis standar. Penggunaan obat ini dipantau secara ketat dan dimaksudkan untuk kenyamanan pasien, bukan untuk merugikan.

**Kesimpulan**

Postingan media sosial yang diperdebatkan ini memperkuat narasi dramatis dan menyedihkan yang tidak didukung oleh bukti yang dapat dipercaya. Meskipun kritik terhadap pengelolaan rumah sakit dan standar perawatan di Romani selama pandemi COVID-19 telah muncul, tidak ada laporan yang terverifikasi bahwa mantan karyawan secara umum mengakui atau menuduh rumah sakit sengaja membunuh pasien untuk memanipulasi statistik kematian korona. Klaim seperti ini tampaknya tidak didasarkan pada fakta dan kemungkinan berkontribusi pada disinformasi serta ketidakpercayaan publik.

Disinformasi dapat menyebar dengan cepat, terutama selama masa krisis. Penting untuk mengandalkan informasi yang terverifikasi dari sumber yang dapat dipercaya dan mempertimbangkan klaim sensasional dengan skeptisisme kecuali mereka didukung oleh bukti yang dapat dipercaya.

article_content:
In recent months, a video collage circulating on social media has drawn attention by juxtaposing footage of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu receiving a COVID-19 vaccination with scenes of a movie prop syringe, highlighting the needle retracting into the barrel. The implication behind the post is that publicly conducted vaccinations, such as Netanyahu’s, may use theatrical devices rather than real injections, thereby questioning the authenticity of high-profile vaccination campaigns and suggesting grounds for mistrust.

Context and Background

Public vaccination campaigns featuring prominent leaders have become a common strategy worldwide to boost public confidence in vaccine safety and efficacy. During the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines, leaders including Benjamin Netanyahu publicly received their shots, often in front of cameras, to encourage citizens to follow suit. Netanyahu’s vaccination was broadcast live in December 2020, with extensive media coverage.

However, skepticism around these events has persisted, fueled by misinformation and doubts about the transparency of such demonstrations. The viral video collage exploits these doubts by drawing a visual parallel between Netanyahu's vaccination and a movie prop syringe, which is designed for use in film and TV productions to simulate injections without actually piercing the skin.

Analysis of the Claim

The core claim in the video collage is that the public vaccinations of leaders may not be authentic and instead could involve theatrical props, such as syringes with retractable or fake needles, thus undermining public trust in vaccination campaigns.

Upon close analysis, the footage of Netanyahu’s vaccination shows a standard medical procedure conducted by a healthcare professional. The process involves swabbing the arm, inserting the needle, and administering the vaccine. There are no obvious signs of a retractable needle or prop syringe, and the vaccination was witnessed by several medical staff and journalists present at the event. While the camera angle and quality do not allow for microscopic scrutiny, there is no credible evidence from the footage or eyewitness accounts to suggest the use of a movie prop.

The comparison with a movie prop syringe is misleading. Prop syringes are specifically designed for staged performances, with needles retracting into the barrel for safety and realism in visual media. Their use in actual medical procedures would not deliver a vaccine or medication. The suggestion that such devices are used in public vaccinations lacks substantiation.

Furthermore, public vaccination events are often conducted in transparent settings, with multiple witnesses and media coverage. The logistics of faking such an event would require complicity from medical professionals and journalists, which is highly unlikely given the scrutiny and accountability mechanisms in place.

Conclusion

The video collage raises questions about the authenticity of public vaccination events by comparing real-life footage with staged movie props. However, there is no credible evidence to support the claim that theatrical devices are used in high-profile vaccinations such as Netanyahu’s. Such comparisons can foster unwarranted mistrust in vaccination campaigns that are crucial for public health. While skepticism and scrutiny of public figures are important, it is equally vital to distinguish between speculation and substantiated concerns, ensuring that misinformation does not undermine efforts to combat the pandemic.

A video circulating on social media has sparked fears and controversy with its claim that a concentration camp is being constructed in Tel Aviv, Israel, specifically for anti-vaxxers. The post suggests that the Israeli government is taking extreme measures to detain individuals who refuse COVID-19 vaccination, drawing parallels to some of the darkest chapters in history. This claim has generated significant attention and alarm, warranting close examination and factual analysis.

First, it is important to understand the context in which this claim has emerged. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, governments worldwide have grappled with balancing public health needs and individual freedoms. Israel, notable for its rapid vaccine rollout, has implemented various measures to encourage vaccination, including public campaigns, incentives, and restrictions for unvaccinated individuals. However, the notion of constructing concentration camps for anti-vaxxers diverges dramatically from the documented policies and practices that have been implemented.

Upon investigation, there is no credible evidence supporting the claim that Israel is building concentration camps in Tel Aviv or anywhere else for anti-vaxxers. The term “concentration camp” carries a heavy historical and emotional burden, especially in the context of Jewish history and the Holocaust. The use of this term in the social media post appears to be aimed at invoking fear and outrage, rather than reflecting reality.

Videos showing construction sites in urban areas often surface online, sometimes stripped of context or accompanied by misleading captions. Fact-checking efforts have consistently found that such videos are frequently misrepresented. In this case, construction activity in Tel Aviv is common due to the city’s ongoing infrastructure and development projects. No official statements from the Israeli government, municipal authorities, or reputable news outlets corroborate the claim that any facility is being erected for the purpose of detaining anti-vaxxers.

Israeli policies regarding COVID-19 vaccination have included the “Green Pass” system, which restricts access to certain venues for the unvaccinated, but these measures do not involve detention or confinement. Legal and ethical standards in Israel, as in most democracies, prohibit the arbitrary detention of citizens on the basis of their medical choices. Furthermore, civil society organizations and the media in Israel operate with considerable freedom, and any attempt to build such a facility would likely provoke widespread public protest and legal challenges.

The video in question lacks identifying features that would indicate it is part of an official government facility, much less a camp for anti-vaxxers. Construction equipment, workers, and fencing are common sights in any major city undergoing development. Without corroborating evidence, it is impossible to substantiate the social media post’s claim.

In conclusion, the assertion that a concentration camp for anti-vaxxers is being constructed in Tel Aviv is unfounded and misleading. It appears to be a sensationalized distortion of ordinary urban development rather than a reflection of actual government policy or practice. As always, it is essential for the public to critically evaluate viral claims and seek out verified information before drawing conclusions.

အောက်ပါ စာရင်းသားသည် စီမံကိန်းကို မီဒီယာကွန်ရက်တွင် ပျံ့နှံ့နေသော ဗီဒီယိုသည် အိုးရိုးများနှင့် အထူးသဖြင့် ထိုက်တန်သော အမျိုးသား အမျိုးသမီးများအား ကာကွယ်ရေးမှားယွင်းသူများအတွက် အစိုးရအဖွဲ့၏ တည်ဆောက်မှုကို ဖော်ပြခြင်းဖြင့် ကြောက်ရွံ့မှုနှင့် အကြွေးရောက်မှုများကို ဖြစ်ပေါ်စေခဲ့သည်။ စာရင်းသားသည် အိုးရိုးများအား ကာကွယ်ရေးမှားယွင်းသူများအား အစိုးရအဖွဲ့က အလွန်ဆိုးရွားသော ဆောင်ရွက်မှုများဖြင့် ဖမ်းဆီးထားသည့်အကြောင်း ဆိုလိုသည်။ ယင်းကို သမိုင်းဝင် အမှုကြီးများကို တွေ့မြင်နိုင်သည့် အမှုကြီးများနှင့် နှိုင်းယှဉ်ကာ အထူးသဖြင့် ဂိုဏ်းဂဏ များကို အဓိကထားသည့် သမိုင်းကြောင်းကို ပြန်လည်သတိရရန် ကြိုးစားခဲ့သည်။ ယင်းကို သတိပြုမှု အများအပြားနှင့် ရောင်းချမှုအများအပြား ဖြစ်ပေါ်ခဲ့ပြီး သတိပြုမှုနှင့် အကြောင်းအရာကို အားကိုးအားထုတ်ခြင်းကို လိုအပ်ပါသည်။

ပထမ အနေဖြင့် ဤအကြောင်းအရာကို ဘယ်လိုသတိပြုမှုအများအပြားကို ရရှိခဲ့သည်ကို နားလည်ရန် အရေးကြီးပါသည်။ ကူးစက်ခြင်း ရောဂါကို ကိုဗစ် ၁၉ တွင် ပြည်နယ်များအနေဖြင့် ကျန်းမာရေး လိုအပ်ချက်များနှင့် အမျိုးသား လိုအပ်ချက်များကို ညှိနှိုင်းရန် အကြံပြုချက်များ ပေးခဲ့သည်။ ထို့အပြင် ကာကွယ်ရေးမှားယွင်းသူများကို အကူအညီပေးခြင်းနှင့် အားလုံးအတွက် တိုးချဲ့ခြင်း ကိုယ်စားပြုခြင်းများကို အစိုးရအဖွဲ့က ပြုလုပ်ခဲ့သည်။ သို့သော် ကာကွယ်ရေးမှားယွင်းသူများအတွက် အစိုးရအဖွဲ့က အစိုးရ အဖွဲ့အစည်းကို ကျော်လွန်ခြင်းနှင့် မတူညီသော အကြောင်းအရာများကို ပြုလုပ်ခြင်းသည် မည်သည့် မှတ်တမ်းတွင် ဖော်ပြခြင်းမရှိသည်။

The COVID-19 pandemic has generated a significant volume of information, some of which is misleading or incorrect. A recent social media post makes five claims regarding mRNA vaccines, Japan’s vaccine policies, the AstraZeneca vaccine, and mortality statistics in Italy. Here is a detailed fact-checking analysis of each claim, with context and background information.

Claim 1: “The technology used in the mRNA coronavirus vaccines was tested only on animals before the pandemic. The RNA-based vaccines have not been tested on humans so far.”

This statement is inaccurate. While mRNA vaccine technology was relatively new in large-scale human applications before COVID-19, it had been tested in humans in clinical trials for other diseases, including certain cancers and infectious diseases, prior to the pandemic. With the emergence of COVID-19, both Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna conducted extensive phase 1, 2, and 3 human clinical trials before their vaccines were authorized for emergency use. These trials involved tens of thousands of volunteer participants and monitored safety, efficacy, and side effects. Therefore, the assertion that RNA-based vaccines had not been tested on humans before their COVID-19 rollout is incorrect.

Claim 2: “Japan suspended use of Moderna vaccine after two cases of anaphylactic shock were reported.”

This claim misrepresents the events in Japan concerning the Moderna vaccine. Japan did temporarily suspend the use of certain batches of the Moderna vaccine in August 2021, but not because of anaphylactic shock reports. The suspension was due to the discovery of contaminants (metal particles) in some vials. While cases of anaphylaxis have been reported globally following COVID-19 vaccination, Japan’s specific suspension was related to concerns over contamination, not anaphylactic reactions.

Claim 3: “The AstraZeneca vaccines arrived in Georgia two weeks earlier and European countries suspended vaccination for two weeks to track the vaccination process in Georgia during next two weeks.”

This claim lacks supporting evidence and seems to conflate unrelated events. AstraZeneca vaccines did arrive in Georgia, but there is no documentation or official announcement that European countries suspended their own AstraZeneca vaccination programs specifically to observe Georgia’s experience. In March 2021, several European countries temporarily paused AstraZeneca vaccinations due to concerns about rare blood clotting events, but these suspensions were based on internal reviews by their own health authorities and not coordinated with Georgia’s rollout.

Claim 4: “AstraZeneca vaccine is ineffective and causes serious side effects. To improve its quality, a trial was conducted in Britain to test combining AstraZeneca and Pfizer vaccines, but it proved unsuccessful.”

This claim is misleading. The AstraZeneca vaccine has been shown to be effective in preventing COVID-19, especially severe illness and hospitalization. While rare side effects, such as blood clots, have been reported, they are extremely uncommon. The assertion that the vaccine is ineffective is not supported by clinical trial data or real-world evidence. Trials combining AstraZeneca and Pfizer vaccines have taken place in the UK and elsewhere, with early results showing that mixing vaccines can produce strong immune responses. There is no evidence that these trials were conducted because AstraZeneca was ineffective, nor that they proved unsuccessful.

Claim 5: “Number of deaths in Italy from December 1, 2019 to April 1, 2020 slightly exceeded number of deaths from December 1, 2018 to April 1, 2019; in fact, it is only by 16 deaths more.”

This claim is false. The COVID-19 pandemic began affecting Italy in early 2020, with a sharp increase in deaths in March 2020. Official mortality data shows a significant excess in deaths during the winter and spring of 2020 compared to previous years. The difference is in the tens of thousands, not 16. The claim severely underestimates the impact of COVID-19 in Italy during this period.

In summary, all five claims made in the social media post are either inaccurate, misleading, or false. Accurate information and careful analysis are essential in understanding the ongoing response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

A social media post claims that Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla has not received the COVID-19 vaccine. This statement has circulated widely, raising questions about the confidence of pharmaceutical leaders in the safety and efficacy of their own products. To assess the veracity of this claim, it is important to examine the timeline of vaccine availability, Bourla’s public statements, and the broader context surrounding vaccine rollouts.

Albert Bourla has been a prominent public face throughout the development and distribution of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. As CEO of Pfizer, Bourla frequently discussed the importance of vaccination, the company’s commitment to safety, and the vaccine’s role in combating the global pandemic. The claim that he has not received the vaccine appears to question his personal trust in the product developed under his leadership.

The origins of this claim can be traced back to December 2020, when the COVID-19 vaccines were first being authorized for emergency use in various countries. At that time, some social media users and commentators noted that Bourla had not yet received his shot, interpreting this as reluctance or a lack of faith in the vaccine. In interviews, Bourla explained that he was adhering to public health guidelines and waiting his turn, as vaccine availability was initially limited and prioritized for frontline healthcare workers, the elderly, and high-risk individuals.

Bourla stated publicly that he did not want to “cut the line” ahead of those most in need. This decision aligned with the ethical standards adopted by many executives and public figures during the early phase of the vaccine rollout, which emphasized equitable access and prioritization based on vulnerability and risk, rather than status or influence.

As vaccine supply increased and eligibility expanded, Bourla did receive his COVID-19 vaccination. He shared this information publicly, using his platform to encourage others to get vaccinated and bolster public confidence in the vaccine’s safety and effectiveness. Subsequent to his initial vaccination, Bourla also reported receiving booster doses, in line with evolving public health recommendations.

The claim that Albert Bourla has not received the COVID-19 vaccine is therefore outdated and misleading. While it is true that he had not been vaccinated in the earliest days of the rollout, this was due to ethical and logistical considerations, not a lack of confidence in the vaccine. Bourla later received the vaccine and has been a vocal proponent of mass vaccination efforts.

In summary, the claim that Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla has not received the COVID-19 vaccine does not accurately reflect the facts. Bourla waited his turn according to public health guidelines and was vaccinated when eligible, using his experience to advocate for vaccination and combat misinformation. Social media users are encouraged to seek current and verified information when evaluating such claims.

Quyết định này phù hợp với các tiêu chuẩn đạo đức được nhiều nhà lãnh đạo và người nổi tiếng áp dụng trong giai đoạn đầu triển khai vaccine, nhấn mạnh việc tiếp cận công bằng và ưu tiên theo mức độ dễ bị tổn thương và rủi ro thay vì theo địa vị hoặc ảnh hưởng.

Do đó, thông tin cho rằng ông Albert Bourla chưa tiêm vaccine ngừa COVID-19 là đã lỗi thời và gây hiểu lầm. Mặc dù đúng là ông chưa tiêm chủng trong những ngày đầu triển khai vaccine, điều này là do các yếu tố đạo đức và logistics, chứ không phải sự thiếu tự tin vào vaccine. article_content:
A social media post circulating in Georgia has raised concerns about the safety of COVID-19 vaccines, specifically alleging that the vaccines introduce gene fragments of RNA into people’s bodies, which will “definitely lead to human genome modification, infertility, cancers and other serious diseases.” The post further claims that official vaccine safety guidance recommends healthy men freeze their sperm before vaccination to avoid infertility. These statements have generated significant anxiety and confusion among the public. A closer examination of the facts behind these claims reveals a stark contrast between scientific evidence and the assertions made in the post.

To understand the core of these concerns, it is important to clarify how mRNA vaccines work. The COVID-19 vaccines developed by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna use messenger RNA (mRNA) technology. This mRNA is a genetic blueprint that instructs cells to produce a harmless piece of the coronavirus spike protein, prompting the immune system to recognize and respond to the real virus. The mRNA never enters the cell’s nucleus, where human DNA is located, and it does not integrate into the genome. After the protein is made, the mRNA fragment is quickly broken down and removed from the body. Concerns about genome modification are therefore unfounded, as mRNA vaccines do not have the capability to alter human DNA.

The post also claims that these vaccines will “definitely” lead to infertility, cancer, and other severe diseases in the near future. To date, extensive clinical trials and ongoing safety monitoring have not found any credible evidence linking COVID-19 vaccines to increased risks of infertility or cancer. Fertility experts and reproductive health organizations have consistently stated that there is no biologically plausible mechanism by which mRNA vaccines could cause infertility in men or women. The assertion that mRNA vaccines cause cancer is also unsupported; the vaccines do not contain any components known to initiate cancerous changes in cells, nor do they persist in the body in a way that would allow such effects to develop.

The statement regarding official vaccine safety guidance is also misleading. The claim that healthy men are advised to freeze their sperm before vaccination is not found in any official vaccine safety manual or guideline. Standard recommendations for COVID-19 vaccination do not include any advice concerning sperm freezing for the general population. Such measures are typically reserved for individuals undergoing medical treatments known to affect fertility, such as chemotherapy, and are not relevant to vaccination.

It is important for the public to be aware that misinformation about vaccines can have serious consequences, including undermining public health efforts and increasing vaccine hesitancy. The development and approval process for COVID-19 vaccines included rigorous testing for safety and efficacy, and ongoing surveillance continues to monitor for rare adverse events. The main side effects reported, such as sore arms, mild fever, or fatigue, are temporary and not considered dangerous.

In summary, the social media post’s claims about genome modification, infertility, cancer, and sperm freezing in relation to COVID-19 vaccines are not supported by scientific evidence or official health guidance. Public health experts encourage individuals to seek accurate information from reliable sources and to consult healthcare professionals with any concerns regarding vaccination.

Επί του παρόντος, οι εκτενείς κλινικές δοκιμές και η συνεχής επιτήρηση ασφαλείας δεν έχουν εντοπίσει καμία πιστή αιτία να συσχετίζεται τα εμβόλια της COVID-19 με αυξημένο κίνδυνο αναπραγμάτευσης ή καρκίνου. Οι ειδικοί στην αναπαραγωγή και οι οργανισμοί υγείας αναπαραγωγής έχουν συνεχώς δηλώσει ότι δεν υπάρχει βιολογικά προσδιορισμένο μηχανισμό με τον οποίο τα εμβόλια mRNA μπορούν να προκαλέσουν αναπραγμάτευση σε άνδρες ή γυναίκες. Η δήλωση ότι τα εμβόλια mRNA προκαλούν καρκίνο είναι επίσης ανεπαρκής, δεν περιέχουν κανένα συστατικό που να αρχίζει αλλοιώσεις καρκινικής φύσεως στα κύτταρα, ούτε παραμένουν στο σώμα με έναν τρόπο που θα επέτρεπε την επίπτωση τέτοιων επιπτώσεων.

Η δήλωση σχετικά με τις προτεινόμενες οδηγίες ασφαλείας εμβολίων είναι επίσης παραπλανητική. Η ισχυριζόμενη ότι οι υγιείς άνδρες συνιστάται να παγώσουν τα σπερματοζωάρια τους πριν από την εμβολιασμό δεν βρίσκεται σε καμία από τις προσωρινές οδηγίες ασφαλείας εμβολίων ή τις προτεινόμενες οδηγίες. Οι προτεινόμενες συστάσεις για την εμβολιασμό κατά της COVID-19 δεν περιλαμβάνουν καμία συστάσεις για την παγώση των σπερματοζωαρίων στο γενικό πληθυσμό. Αυτές οι μέτρα είναι συνήθως καταχωρισμένες για άτομα που υποβάλλονται σε ιατρικές θεραπείες που γνωστικά επηρεάζουν την αναπαραγωγή, όπως η χημειοθεραπεία, και δεν είναι σχετικές με την εμβολιασμό.

Είναι σημαντικό να είναι συνειδητό για το κοινό ότι η παραπλανητική πληροφορία σχετικά με τα εμβόλια μπορεί να έχει σοβαρές συνέπειες, συμπεριλαμβανομένων της παρατροπής των προσπαθειών για τη δημόσια υγεία και της αύξησης της αποστασιοποίησης από τα εμβόλια. Το διαδικαστικό ανάπτυξης και της εγκρίσεως των εμβολίων της COVID-19 περιλαμβάνει αυστηρό έλεγχο για την ασφάλεια και την αποτελεσματικότητα, και η συνεχής επιτήρηση συνεχίζει να επιτηρεί τις σπάνιες αρνητικές επιπτώσεις. Οι κύριες παρενέργειες που αναφέρονται, όπως πόνος στα χέρια, ελαφρύ πυρετό ή κατάποση, είναι προσωρινές και δεν θεωρούνται επικίνδυνες.

Συνοπτικά, οι δηλώσεις της αναρτήσεως σχετικά με την τροποποίηση του γονιδιώματος, την αναπραγμάτευση, τον καρκίνο και την παγώση των σπερματοζωαρίων σε σχέση με τα εμβόλια της COVID-19 δεν υποστηρίζονται από επιστημονικά ευρετήρια ή προσωρινές οδηγίες υγείας. Οι επιστημονικοί παράγοντες της δημόσιας υγείας ενθαρρύνουν τους ανθρώπους να ζητήσουν ακριβή πληροφορίες από αξιόπιστες πηγές και να συμβουλευτούν επαγγελματίες υγείας με οποιαδήποτε ανησυχία σχετικά με την εμβολιασμό.

On social media, a post has circulated claiming that a protest was held against vaccination in Amsterdam. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine recent events in Amsterdam, provide context related to vaccination debates in the Netherlands, and analyze the available evidence regarding public demonstrations.

Protests and public demonstrations have been a prominent part of the global response to the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in relation to government policies on vaccination, lockdowns, and other public health measures. The Netherlands, known for its strong tradition of public assembly and free speech, has witnessed a number of protests on a variety of issues over the past several years, including those relating to vaccination requirements and pandemic response.

In Amsterdam, the capital city, there have been documented instances of protests associated with opposition to COVID-19 vaccination policies. These demonstrations have typically attracted a diverse group of participants, including individuals skeptical of vaccine mandates, people concerned about government overreach, and some with broader anti-establishment views. Common themes at such protests include calls for bodily autonomy, opposition to vaccine passports, and demands for the restoration of certain civil liberties that were restricted during the pandemic.

Fact-checking the specific claim that a protest against vaccination was held in Amsterdam involves examining news reports, photographic evidence, and statements from local authorities. During the height of the COVID-19 vaccination rollout—particularly in 2021 and 2022—Amsterdam saw several large-scale protests at central locations such as Museumplein and Dam Square. These events drew national and international attention, and in some cases required police intervention due to the size of the crowds or breaches of public order regulations.

While the majority of recent protests have focused on anti-mandate sentiments rather than opposition to vaccines themselves, anti-vaccination viewpoints were nonetheless represented at many of these gatherings. Protesters often carried signs expressing skepticism about vaccine safety, government transparency, and the perceived infringement of personal freedoms. Organizers used social media to publicize these events and mobilize support, which likely contributed to the spread of claims like the one under review.

It is important to note that the scale and tone of these protests varied widely. Some were peaceful and involved a relatively small number of participants, while others were larger and more confrontational. Local authorities, including the Amsterdam police, routinely issued statements to encourage peaceful assembly and to remind participants of applicable regulations.

In conclusion, the claim that a protest against vaccination was held in Amsterdam is supported by available evidence. Multiple protests related to opposition to vaccination policies, mandates, and pandemic restrictions have taken place in the city since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic. These events have included participants with anti-vaccination views, confirming the core assertion of the social media post. However, it is also clear that many of the demonstrations encompassed broader themes beyond opposition to vaccination itself. The context of ongoing public debate and evolving health policies in the Netherlands is essential to understanding the nature and motivations of such protests.

article_content:
The rapid rollout of COVID-19 vaccines sparked widespread debate and scrutiny, especially around the safety profiles of vaccines such as AstraZeneca, Moderna, and Pfizer-BioNTech. A recent social media post claims that “72%, 49%, and 30% of severe effects were recorded following vaccinations with AstraZeneca, Moderna, and Pfizer respectively.” This statement implies that the risk of severe side effects varies dramatically between these vaccines, with AstraZeneca purportedly having the highest rate.

To evaluate the accuracy of this claim, it is crucial to clarify what is meant by “severe effects,” understand how such data is collected and reported, and compare these numbers to official sources.

First, “severe effects” generally refer to adverse events following immunization (AEFIs) that require medical attention, hospitalization, or result in significant disability. Examples include severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis), blood clotting disorders, myocarditis, or other life-altering conditions. Vaccine safety data is meticulously collected through clinical trials and ongoing pharmacovigilance systems, with adverse events categorized as mild, moderate, or severe.

The three vaccines referenced—AstraZeneca’s Vaxzevria, Moderna’s Spikevax, and Pfizer-BioNTech’s Comirnaty—were subjected to rigorous testing before approval and have since been administered to hundreds of millions globally. Surveillance data consistently indicate that all three vaccines are safe and that the incidence of severe side effects is rare.

The post’s figures—72% for AstraZeneca, 49% for Moderna, and 30% for Pfizer—are ambiguous. The percentages could suggest that out of all vaccinated individuals, these proportions experienced severe side effects, or that among those who did experience any side effects, these percentages were severe. Both interpretations would be misleading. In published safety data, the overall incidence of severe side effects is below 1% for all three vaccines. For instance, common side effects such as fatigue, headache, or mild fever are frequently reported, but severe reactions are exceedingly rare.

Furthermore, there has been focused attention on specific risks associated with each vaccine. AstraZeneca’s vaccine was scrutinized for rare blood clotting events, particularly cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, but these occurred in an estimated 1 to 2 cases per 100,000 recipients—far less than the 72% indicated. Moderna and Pfizer vaccines have been linked to rare cases of myocarditis, mainly in young males, but again, these rates are in the range of several cases per 100,000 doses. No data supports the assertion that nearly a third or more of recipients experience severe effects with any of these vaccines.

It is possible that the percentages in the post stem from a misinterpretation of data, such as the proportion of severe events among all reported adverse reactions, not among all vaccinated individuals. Even then, these proportions are inflated compared to official reports, where most adverse events are mild or moderate.

In summary, the claim that 72%, 49%, and 30% of severe effects were recorded with AstraZeneca, Moderna, and Pfizer vaccines, respectively, does not align with the available evidence. Vaccine safety monitoring indicates that severe side effects are very rare for all three, and the benefits of vaccination far outweigh the risks. Misinformation about vaccine safety can undermine public trust and vaccine uptake, making accurate communication essential as the world continues to manage COVID-19.
